module-4-quick-review-optional.title: Module 4 Quick Review (optional)
module-4-quick-review-optional.body:
Optional quick review, about a two-minute read. Not graded. For more detail, see the full Chapter Review page.

Formulas to know
  • ROE = net income ÷ average stockholders’ equity
  • ROA = net income ÷ average total assets
  • Financial leverage = average total assets ÷ average equity
  • ROE = ROA × financial leverage
  • ROA = profit margin × asset turnover
  • NOA = operating assets − operating liabilities
  • RNOA = NOPAT ÷ average NOA = net operating profit margin × net operating asset turnover

1. Return on equity (ROE)

  • ROE = net income ÷ average stockholders’ equity. It measures the return from the owners’ point of view.
  • Use the average of beginning and ending equity, because equity changes during the year.
  • Compare ROE across years and with peers. A fall in ROE is a signal to ask which driver changed.

2. DuPont analysis: ROE = ROA × financial leverage

  • ROA = net income ÷ average total assets. Financial leverage = average total assets ÷ average equity.
  • ROE = ROA × financial leverage.
  • Higher leverage can raise ROE when assets earn more than the cost of debt, but it also raises risk, because debt payments are mandatory.

3. ROA = profit margin × asset turnover

  • Profit margin = net income ÷ net sales. Asset turnover = net sales ÷ average total assets.
  • ROA = profit margin × asset turnover.
  • A thin margin can be offset by high turnover, and the reverse. Compare a company with a peer on both parts.

4. Why ROE fell when sales grew

  • Profitability: gross profit margin (gross profit ÷ sales) and operating expense margin show whether growth turned into profit.
  • Productivity: assets that grow faster than sales lower asset turnover. Here, the new plant, the acquisition and a large cash balance enlarged assets.
  • A larger equity base (the April share sale) lowers ROE when income does not grow with it.

5. Operating and nonoperating items, and net operating assets (NOA)

  • Operating items arise from making and selling products: receivables, inventories, property and equipment, intangibles, payables, accrued liabilities, warranty and deferred revenue.
  • Nonoperating items come from financing and investing: cash and investments, and interest-bearing debt.
  • NOA = operating assets − operating liabilities. Equivalent: equity + interest-bearing debt − cash.

6. NOPAT and return on net operating assets (RNOA)

  • NOPAT = operating profit after tax. Interest and other nonoperating items are left out, and the tax on operating profit excludes the tax shield from interest.
  • RNOA = NOPAT ÷ average NOA = net operating profit margin × net operating asset turnover.
  • The lecture compares RNOA with the median for S&P 500 firms (13.5% in 2022).

7. Common-size statements and horizontal analysis

  • Vertical (common-size) analysis: express each line as a percent of net sales (income statement) or total assets (balance sheet).
  • Horizontal analysis: growth = (this year − last year) ÷ last year.
  • Ratios have limits: accounting rules omit many assets, mergers change comparability, and one number cannot capture everything.

LO 4-1 Return on Equity (ROE)

  • ROE is the most common analysis metric used by managers and investors alike.
  • It relates net income to average total stockholders’ equity and measures return from the stockholders’ perspective.
ROE = Net income ÷ Average stockholders’ equity

Pfizer, 2022: ROE = $31,372 ÷ [($95,661 + $77,201) ÷ 2] = $31,372 ÷ $86,431 = 36.3%. For comparison, ROE for S&P 500 companies ranged from 13.7% to 17.3% over 2018–2022.

Which accounts to use

SituationROE formula
Noncontrolling interestNet income attributable to company shareholders ÷ Average equity attributable to company shareholders
Preferred stock(Net income attributable to company shareholders − Preferred dividends) ÷ (Average equity attributable to company shareholders − Average preferred equity)

Occidental Petroleum, 2022 (preferred stock of $9,762 both years): net income $13,304 − preferred dividends $800 = $12,504 to common stockholders. ROE = $12,504 ÷ [($30,085 − $9,762) + ($20,327 − $9,762)] ÷ 2 = $12,504 ÷ $15,444 = 81%.

LO 4-2 DuPont Disaggregation: ROA and Financial Leverage

There are two ways to measure the drivers of ROE: (1) traditional DuPont analysis, which splits ROE into profitability, productivity, and leverage; and (2) operating-focus analysis, which separates operating from nonoperating activities (LOs 4-4 to 4-8).

DuPont disaggregation
ROE = ROA × Financial leverage (FL) × NCIR
= (Net income ÷ Avg. total assets) × (Avg. total assets ÷ Avg. stockholders’ equity) × NCIR
NCIR = 1 for companies with no noncontrolling interest.
  • ROE reflects both company performance (ROA) and how the assets are financed (FL).
  • For a given level of assets, ROE is higher with more debt and less equity — but more debt means more risk.

Return on assets (ROA)

ROA = Net income ÷ Average total assets
  • ROA measures return from the perspective of the entire company (the enterprise level).
  • The numerator comes from the income statement and the denominator from the balance sheet, so a high ROA requires being profitable and managing assets — ROA pushes managers to focus on both statements.

Pfizer: ROA = $31,407 ÷ [($197,205 + $181,476) ÷ 2] = $31,407 ÷ $189,341 = 16.6%. The median S&P 500 ROA was 6.1% in 2022 (range 4.4%–6.4% over 2018–2022).

Financial leverage (FL)

FL = Average total assets ÷ Average stockholders’ equity
  • FL measures the degree to which the company finances its assets with debt versus equity. (There are many leverage measures; this one is FL. LO 4-8 introduces FLEV.)
  • Leverage matters because debt is a contractual obligation — failing to pay interest or principal has legal consequences. All else equal, higher leverage raises the probability of default and bankruptcy.

Pfizer: FL = $189,341 ÷ [($95,916 + $77,462) ÷ 2] = $189,341 ÷ $86,689 = 2.18. The median S&P 500 FL was about 2.5–2.6 over 2018–2022.

Noncontrolling interest ratio (NCIR)

Most S&P 500 companies report some noncontrolling interest. Because ROE focuses on the company’s common shareholders, a third term adjusts for the two shareholder groups:

NCIR = (NI attributable to common shareholders ÷ Net income) ÷ (Avg. equity attributable to common shareholders ÷ Avg. total equity)

Pfizer: NCIR = ($31,372 ÷ $31,407) ÷ ($86,431 ÷ $86,689) = 1.00188.

Pfizer’s DuPont check
ROE = 16.59% × 2.184 × 1.00188 = 36.3%
Because most companies have NCIR close to 1, ROE ≈ ROA × FL is usually a good approximation.

LO 4-3 Disaggregating ROA: Profitability and Productivity

ROA = Profit margin (PM) × Asset turnover (AT)
= (Net income ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Average total assets)
  • Profit margin — what the company earns on each sales dollar.
  • Asset turnover — the sales generated from each dollar invested in assets.
  • Managers raise ROA by increasing PM (more profit for a given level of assets), increasing AT (fewer assets for the same profit), or both.

Pfizer: PM = $31,407 ÷ $100,330 = 31.3%; AT = $100,330 ÷ $189,341 = 0.53; ROA = 31.3% × 0.53 = 16.6%.

Adjusted ROA
Operating managers control ROA, but not the capital structure. Analysts therefore often add back the after-tax net interest expense (net of interest revenue and other nonoperating items) to the numerator:
Adjusted ROA = [Net income + Net interest expense × (1 − Statutory tax rate)] ÷ Average total assets
Pfizer: [$31,407 + ($987 − $997) × (1 − 0.22)] ÷ $189,340.5 = $31,399.2 ÷ $189,340.5 = 16.58%. The statutory rate (22%) is the assumed combined federal and state rate. The adjusted numerator approximates NOPAT (LO 4-5).

Two levels of analysis

Splitting ROE into ROA and FL is the first level. The second level looks for the factors behind profitability and productivity. ROE increases with each component.

Analyzing productivity: working capital

The cash conversion cycle is the average number of days to buy inventory on credit, sell it on credit, collect the receivables, and pay the suppliers. Companies generally prefer a lower CCC, because the operating cycle then generates profit and cash quickly. Analyze the CCC over time and against peers with similar business models. The S&P 500 CCC has ranged from roughly 47 to 53 days over 2013–2022.

A company’s CCC depends on its business model: the credit terms it offers customers, the kinds of inventory it carries and the depth and breadth of its product lines, and how quickly it pays suppliers. Median CCC is shortest in energy and longest in healthcare (over 100 days).

Analyzing productivity: PP&E

PP&E turnover = Sales ÷ Average PP&E. (Pfizer: $100,330 ÷ [($16,274 + $14,882) ÷ 2] = 6.4 times.) Improving PP&E turnover is not easy; it often involves:

  • Divesting unproductive assets or entire business lines
  • Joint ventures to share PP&E such as distribution networks, IT, production facilities, and warehouses
  • Selling production facilities while agreeing to buy finished goods from the new owners
  • Sale and leaseback of administrative buildings

Analyzing financial leverage

  • Used judiciously, leverage benefits stockholders — debt is a relatively inexpensive source of capital — but it adds risk, because repayment is mandatory.
  • Leverage analysis typically examines (1) the level of borrowed money relative to equity (e.g., total debt-to-equity) and (2) the level of profit or cash flow relative to required debt payments (e.g., times interest earned).
When equity is near zero or negative
Stock buybacks have grown dramatically, leaving many balance sheets with large treasury stock or very low retained earnings. A small equity balance in the denominator inflates ROE.
Apple, 2018–2022: net income totaled $366.7 billion while buybacks totaled $409.1 billion. Buybacks plus a large negative AOCI balance cut stockholders’ equity from $107.1 billion to $50.7 billion, lifting ROE from 49% to 176%.
Analysts respond by using measures less sensitive to small equity: a ROA focus or a financial leverage focus.

LO 4-4 Net Operating Assets (NOA)

Why an operating focus?

  • Companies create value mainly through their core operations, but both the balance sheet and income statement mix operating and nonoperating items.
  • Analysis improves when we separate the operating and nonoperating components and measure their returns separately:
ROE = Operating return + Nonoperating return
Operating return comes from sales, expenses, and so on; nonoperating return comes from financing and investing activities.

In DuPont analysis, FL (Total assets ÷ Equity) lumps all liabilities together. The operating approach splits them:

Operating assets include accounts receivable, unbilled revenues, credit card and other financing receivables (for many companies), inventories, prepaid expenses, PP&E, right-of-use assets, natural resources, equity-method investments, goodwill and intangibles, and deferred tax assets. Operating liabilities include accounts payable, accrued liabilities, deferred revenue, pension and other post-employment liabilities, and deferred tax liabilities. All equity accounts, including noncontrolling interest, are equity.

Classifying leases

  • Many companies lease buildings and equipment rather than buy them. Economically, leasing is no different from buying the asset with borrowed money.
  • So the right-of-use asset is an operating asset, and the related lease obligation is a nonoperating liability.
  • The challenge: some balance sheets do not report lease items separately, so analysts must dig into the notes.

Appendix 4A: classifying income statement items

Typical nonoperating income statement items for nonfinancial companies: interest expense; gains and losses on debt retirement; interest and dividend revenue; investment gains and losses; the tax shield on net nonoperating expense; and income (loss) from discontinued operations, net of tax. Revenues, cost of sales, and operating expenses — SG&A, depreciation and amortization, restructuring, R&D, asset impairments, and gains or losses on disposals of PP&E and other operating assets — are operating, as is income from equity-method investments.

RNOA = NOPAT ÷ Average NOA
Average NOA = (NOA at start of year + NOA at end of year) ÷ 2

module-5-quick-review-optional.title: Module 5 Quick Review (optional)
module-5-quick-review-optional.body:
Optional quick review, about a two-minute read. Not graded. For more detail, see the full Chapter Review page.

Formulas to know
  • Net sales = gross sales − returns, allowances and rebates
  • Net receivables = gross receivables − allowance
  • Ending allowance = beginning + bad debt expense − write-offs
  • DSO = 365 ÷ (net sales ÷ average net receivables)
  • Ending deferred revenue = beginning + billed in advance − revenue recognized
  • Dollar sales = foreign currency sales × average exchange rate

1. Revenue recognition and net sales

  • Revenue is recognized when the company transfers the good or service to the customer, even if cash has not arrived.
  • Companies deduct expected returns, allowances and rebates from gross sales to report net sales, and they estimate these when they record the sale.
  • Estimating at the time of the sale matches the cost of returns to the period of the sale.

2. Sales returns and allowances as a percent of gross sales

  • Returns and rebates ÷ gross sales measures the income statement effect of pricing pressure.
  • A rising percentage lowers net sales at any given level of gross sales.
  • Compare actual returns with earlier estimates to check whether the estimates were adequate.

3. Receivables and the allowance for doubtful accounts

  • The allowance is a contra-asset: net receivables = gross receivables − allowance.
  • Bad debt expense raises the allowance and lowers net income. A write-off lowers gross receivables and the allowance equally, so net receivables and net income do not change.
  • Rollforward: beginning allowance + bad debt expense − write-offs = ending allowance.

4. Receivables turnover and days sales outstanding (DSO)

  • Receivables turnover = net sales ÷ average net receivables. DSO = 365 ÷ turnover.
  • Receivables growing faster than sales shows a lower turnover, a longer DSO and a possible decline in credit quality.
  • Collecting faster raises operating cash flow.

5. Deferred (unearned) revenue

  • Deferred revenue is a liability: the company has the cash but still owes the service.
  • Rollforward: beginning + billed in advance − revenue recognized = ending.
  • A shrinking balance can warn of lower future revenue; a growing one suggests new prepayments.

6. Foreign currency and sales in euros

  • Translate foreign sales at the average exchange rate: euros × dollars per euro.
  • A weaker foreign currency (stronger dollar) lowers reported dollar sales; a stronger foreign currency raises them.
  • Analysts compute ratios with and without currency effects because those effects are unpredictable.

LO 5-1 Revenue Recognition

Revenue recognition at Pfizer

From Pfizer's revenue recognition policy note: "We record revenues from product sales when there is a transfer of control of the product from us to the customer. We determine transfer of control based on when the product is shipped or delivered and title passes to the customer . . . Our gross product revenues are subject to a variety of deductions, which generally are estimated and recorded in the same period that the revenues are recognized. Such variable consideration represents chargebacks, rebates, sales allowances, and sales returns."

Chargebacks, rebates, sales allowances, and sales returns are deducted from GROSS REVENUE.

Four issues drive the analysis of revenue for a company like Pfizer:

  • Revenue recognition timing
  • Sales and related allowances
  • Deferred revenue — advance payments from customers
  • Foreign currency exchange rates

Sales on credit

  • Many sales are on credit, meaning the customer has agreed to pay the company in the future.
  • The company recognizes revenue when the good or service is transferred to the customer, and records an account receivable to be collected later.
  • Revenue recognition is unaffected by the delayed receipt of cash if the company has fulfilled its performance obligation.

The five-step revenue recognition rule

StepWhat it requires
1. Identify the contract(s) with the customerParties to the contract should be identifiable; terms of the sale should be specified.
2. Identify the performance obligation(s) in the contractA performance obligation is a contractual promise to transfer a good or service to the customer. For contracts with more than one good or service, the company must identify separate performance obligations for each contractual promise.
3. Determine the transaction priceIf the selling price is variable, estimate revenue using the expected selling price.
4. Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligation(s)With more than one performance obligation, allocate the transaction price to each at its fair value (standalone selling price). If standalone prices are not available, use a reasonable estimate.
5. Recognize revenue as / when each performance obligation is satisfiedA performance obligation is satisfied when the customer obtains control of the goods or services. Obligations satisfied over a period of time are recognized as revenue over time.

Complications of revenue recognition

SituationWhen revenue is recognized
Right of returnEstimate the amount likely to be returned and deduct it to arrive at NET sales.
Gift cardsWhen the gift card is used by the customer.
Nonrefundable up-front feesWhen the future goods or services are provided.
Bill-and-hold arrangementsWhen control of the goods transfers to the customer.
Consignment salesIf the seller acts as an agent, recognize the commission.
LicensesDepends on the contract: right to use — recognize when the customer can first use the licensed IP; promise of access — recognize over a period of time.
FranchisesGoods component when the goods are transferred to the buyer; services component (use of trade name or license) as the services are delivered.
Variable considerationRecognize the expected amount to be received when goods or services are provided.
Multiple element contractsSeparate the sale into distinct goods and services valued on a stand-alone basis, and recognize revenue separately on each distinct component.
Performance obligations satisfied over time: the cost-to-cost method
Percentage complete = Costs incurred to date ÷ Total estimated costs at completion
Revenue recognized = Contract price × Percentage complete
  • Revenue is recognized over the life of a long-term contract in amounts that track the percentage of completion.
  • If a company incurs 15% of the total expected cost in the current period, it recognizes revenues equal to 15% of the contract amount.

Raytheon's 2022 disclosure: "For performance obligations satisfied over time, revenue is recognized on a percentage of completion basis generally using costs incurred to date relative to total estimated costs at completion to measure progress."

LO 5-3 Unearned (Deferred) Revenue

  • In some industries it is common to receive cash before recording revenue. Deposits or advance payments are not recorded as revenue until the company performs the services owed or delivers the goods.
  • The company must record a liability (unearned revenue) because it is obligated to deliver those products and services.
  • When the good is provided or the service rendered, the unearned revenue liability is reduced and revenue is recognized.
  • Unearned revenue is particularly common among companies that receive advance payments, sell gift cards, or sell memberships or subscriptions.

Walmart's policy note illustrates all three: net sales are recognized net of sales taxes and estimated sales returns at the time merchandise or services are sold; membership fee revenue is recognized over the term of the membership, typically 12 months, with deferred membership fee revenue included in accrued liabilities; gift cards are not recognized as sales until the card is redeemed; and revenue from financial and other services is recognized when the service is performed.

Analysis of unearned revenue

  • If deferred revenue liabilities decrease, we infer that current reported revenue was collected from customers in a prior period — there have been fewer new prepayments for which revenue will be recognized in the future. Such a trend could predict future declines in revenue and profit.
  • Growth in deferred revenue could predict future increases in revenue and profit.
  • In either case, pay attention to the rate of increase or decrease as well as to the dollar amount of the change during the period.

LO 5-4 Foreign Currency Exchange Rates

Accounting for foreign currency effects

  • Companies routinely conduct business in foreign currencies. Foreign subsidiaries transact almost entirely in their home currencies and maintain their accounting records in those currencies.
  • Before the subsidiaries' financial statements are consolidated, they must be translated into $US.
  • As the $US strengthens against other world currencies, each unit of foreign currency buys less in $US terms. When a foreign subsidiary's income statement is translated, every income statement item shrinks — reported revenues and expenses are smaller than before the $US strengthened. The balance sheet shrinks as well, giving lower $US values for assets, liabilities, and equity.

Foreign currency effects at Pfizer

Pfizer's MD&A reported: "Revenues increased 23% in 2022 reflecting an operational increase of 30%, as well as an unfavorable impact of foreign exchange of 7%." We can infer that the $US dollar strengthened during the year.

Pfizer also discloses that 58% of its total 2022 revenues were derived from international operations, including 26% from Europe and 20% from Japan, China, and the rest of the Asia Pacific region.

  • Foreign currency effects are largely translation, not transaction, effects. It is only the $US equivalent that changes with fluctuating exchange rates, not the underlying operating cash flows.

  • Using the income statement as reported implicitly includes the foreign currency effects.

R&D costs broadly consist of: salaries and benefits for researchers and developers; supplies needed to conduct the research; licensing fees for intellectual property or software used in the R&D process; third-party payments to collaborators at other firms and universities; laboratory and other equipment; and property and buildings used as research facilities.

R&D costs are expensed as incurred, except for general-purpose PP&E assets, which are capitalized and depreciated as usual.

Why segregate discontinued operations?

  • Discontinued operations are segregated because they represent a transitory item. Transitory items will not recur and are therefore largely irrelevant to predicting future performance.
  • Investors tend to focus on income from continuing operations, because that is the level of profitability likely to persist into the future.
  • To be classified as a discontinued operation, the disposal of the business unit must represent a strategic shift for the company and have a major effect on the company's financial results.

Several numbers could be used to analyze company performance; which one we use depends on the question we seek to answer.

LO 5-7 Pro Forma and Non-GAAP Disclosures

Pro forma income reporting

  • Pro forma income statements are non-GAAP numbers that company management believes provide a better measure of their financial performance.
  • The SEC requires that companies reconcile non-GAAP information to GAAP numbers (Regulation G).
  • Remember that a company's purpose in making a non-GAAP disclosure is to portray its financial performance the way management would like us to analyze it. Unscrupulous companies might attempt to present results in the best possible light (opportunism).

Pro forma disclosure at Pfizer. Pfizer's 2022 earnings release reported full-year revenues of $100.3 billion reflecting 30% operational growth (excluding Paxlovid and Comirnaty, revenues grew 2% operationally), and full-year reported diluted EPS of $5.47, up 42%, alongside adjusted diluted EPS of $6.58, up 62%.

  • Adjusted diluted EPS is not a GAAP metric.
  • Pfizer made a number of deductions and additions to its GAAP numbers because management believes doing so provides a better measure of financial performance.
  • Adjusted income statements are sometimes referred to as pro forma or non-GAAP numbers.

SEC warning on pro forma information

The SEC cautions public companies on the use of "pro forma" financial information and alerts investors to its potential dangers. Its key points:

  • In this context the term has no defined meaning and no uniform characteristics.
  • Pro forma information can serve useful purposes — focusing investors' attention on critical components of results, providing meaningful comparison to prior periods, or emphasizing the results of core operations. There is no prohibition on publishing interpretations or summaries of GAAP results.
  • Nonetheless, pro forma information can mislead investors if it obscures GAAP results. Because it departs from traditional accounting conventions, its use can make it hard to compare an issuer's information with other reporting periods and with other companies.
  • The SEC's advice: compare any summary or pro forma presentation with the results reported on GAAP-based financials by the same company. "Read before you invest; understand before you commit."

Disclosures and Market Assessments

For a thorough reading of the GAAP financials:

  • Read the external audit report and note any deviation from boilerplate language
  • Peruse notes on accounting policies and compare with industry peers
  • Examine changes in accounting policies
  • Compare key ratios over time
  • Review ratios of competitors and consider how macroeconomic conditions have shifted ratios over time
  • Identify nonrecurring items and separately assess their impact on company performance and position

module-6-quick-review-optional.title: Module 6 Quick Review (optional)
module-6-quick-review-optional.body:
Optional quick review, about a two-minute read. Not graded. For more detail, see the full Chapter Review page.

Formulas to know
  • COGS = cost of goods available for sale − ending inventory
  • Average cost = total cost available ÷ total units available
  • Annual straight-line depreciation = (cost − salvage) ÷ useful life
  • Goodwill = purchase price − fair value of identifiable net assets
  • DPO = 365 ÷ (COGS ÷ average accounts payable)
  • Cash conversion cycle = DIO + DSO − DPO

1. Cost flow and FIFO

  • Inventory cost is capitalized (an asset) and moves to cost of goods sold when the goods are sold.
  • Cost of goods available for sale = beginning inventory + purchases. COGS = cost available − ending inventory.
  • FIFO: the oldest costs go to COGS first, so ending inventory holds the newest costs.

2. LIFO and the effect of rising costs

  • LIFO: the newest costs go to COGS first, so ending inventory holds the oldest costs.
  • When costs are rising, LIFO has a higher COGS, lower gross profit, lower taxes and an older, lower inventory value.
  • Companies using LIFO must disclose the FIFO equivalent (the LIFO reserve). Taxes often drive the choice of LIFO.

3. Weighted-average cost

  • Average cost = total cost available ÷ total units available.
  • Ending inventory and COGS are each priced at the average.
  • With rising costs, average cost lands between FIFO and LIFO.

4. Capitalize or expense?

  • Property, plant and equipment is recorded at cost, including freight, taxes, installation and testing needed to put it into service.
  • Training, routine maintenance and repairs are expensed when incurred.
  • Expenditures for PP&E are called CAPEX.

5. Straight-line depreciation

  • Annual depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life.
  • Depreciation lowers net PP&E through accumulated depreciation (a contra-asset) and is an expense with no cash effect.
  • For a partial year, multiply by the fraction of the year the asset was in use.

6. Goodwill and acquired technology

  • Goodwill = purchase price − fair value of identifiable net assets (including identified intangibles such as technology).
  • Goodwill is not amortized; it is tested for impairment at least once a year.
  • Identified intangibles with a limited life, such as acquired technology, are amortized over their lives.

7. Days payables and the cash conversion cycle

  • DPO = 365 ÷ payables turnover, where payables turnover = COGS ÷ average accounts payable.
  • Cash conversion cycle = DIO + DSO − DPO. A shorter cycle frees cash.
  • Paying suppliers very late (“leaning on the trade”) can damage supplier relationships.

Because each of these involves choices and estimates, two companies with identical economics can report very different numbers — which is why the disclosures and the ratios in this module matter.

LO 6-1 Inventory Costing Methods

Flow of costs

  • When inventory is purchased or produced, it is capitalized on the balance sheet.
  • When the inventory is sold, its cost is transferred from the balance sheet to the income statement as COGS.

Capitalization of inventory cost

  • Capitalization means that a cost is recorded on the balance sheet and is not immediately expensed in the income statement.
  • For purchased inventories, the amount capitalized is the purchase price.
  • For manufactured inventory, we capitalize all manufacturing costs, which consist of three components:
  • Cost of direct (raw) materials used in the product
  • Cost of direct labor to manufacture the product
  • Manufacturing overhead

Cost of goods sold

Beginning inventory + Inventory acquired = Cost of goods available for sale
Cost of goods available for sale = Ending inventory + Cost of goods sold
  • Beginning inventory is the ending inventory balance of the prior period.
  • Current inventory purchases (or manufacturing costs) are added to the beginning balance, yielding the cost of goods available for sale.
  • Goods available are either sold and flow to COGS, or the goods remain unsold and are in inventory at the end of the period.

Gross profit and managerial choice

Sales − Cost of goods sold = Gross profit
  • If higher cost units are transferred from the balance sheet, then COGS is higher and gross profit is lower.
  • If lower cost units are transferred to COGS, gross profit is higher.
  • Companies have a choice when it comes to determining COGS and the cost of the inventory remaining on the balance sheet.
  • Three choices for inventory costing: FIFO, LIFO, and average cost.

LO 6-4 Capitalization and Depreciation of Tangible Assets

PP&E: capitalization and depreciation

  • When PP&E is acquired, it is recorded at cost on the balance sheet. This is called capitalization — which is why expenditures for PP&E are called CAPEX.
  • The amount capitalized includes all costs to put the asset into service: the PP&E cost as well as transportation, duties, tax, and the necessary costs to install and test the assets.
  • Once capitalized, the PP&E cost is recognized as expense over the period of time that the PP&E produces revenues. Depreciation recognizes the using up of the asset over its useful life.
  • Instead of purchasing PP&E outright, companies often enter into long-term equipment leases. If the lease terms extend beyond a year, the equipment is capitalized just like other tangible assets.

Depreciation expense assumptions

To determine depreciation expense, a company makes three estimates:

EstimateDefinition
Useful lifeThe period of time over which the asset is expected to generate measurable benefits
Salvage valueThe amount expected for the asset when disposed of at the end of its useful life
Depreciation methodAn estimate of how the asset is used up over its useful life

Straight-line method

Assume a company acquires a machine for $100,000 with a $10,000 salvage value and a 5-year useful life.

Depreciation baseDepreciation rate
Cost − Salvage value = $100,000 − $10,000 = $90,0001 ÷ Estimated useful life = 1 ÷ 5 years = 20%

With the straight-line (SL) method, $18,000 of depreciation expense is recognized per year over the asset's estimated useful life:

Depreciation expense per year = $90,000 ÷ 5 = $18,000

The accumulated depreciation (contra asset) account increases by $18,000, thus reducing net PP&E by the same amount. At the end of the 1st year the asset is reported on the balance sheet as:

Other depreciation methods

  • Accelerated depreciation methods record more depreciation in the early years of an asset's useful life (hence "accelerated") and less in later years.
  • The units-of-production method records depreciation according to asset use. The depreciation base is cost less salvage value; the depreciation rate is the units produced and sold during the year compared with the total expected units to be produced and sold.
  • The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS), an accelerated method, is required by the U.S. IRS to calculate taxable income.

R&D facilities and equipment

  • R&D facilities and equipment are not immediately expensed. If they are general-use in nature, costs are capitalized on the balance sheet and depreciated over their useful life like other depreciable assets.
  • R&D facilities and equipment purchased specifically for a single R&D project, with no alternative use, are expensed immediately.
  • R&D costs do create future benefits and might seem to be assets — but R&D costs are not capitalized:
  • Whether any tangible products or services will be developed is often uncertain; many R&D efforts fail to produce any benefits whatsoever.
  • Even for promising R&D programs, the timing of future products and services is uncertain.
  • Salaries for R&D personnel are no different from those of other personnel, whose salaries and wages are expensed when incurred.

LO 6-7 Intangible Assets

Acquiring intangible assets

  • When one company acquires another, we must allocate the purchase price to the assets acquired and the liabilities assumed.
  • After the purchase price is allocated, any excess is allocated to the acquired intangible assets.
  • Each intangible asset must be identified, valued, and assigned a useful life, just like PP&E.
  • Intangibles can comprise a large proportion of a company's balance sheet: intangible assets as a percent of total assets for S&P 500 nonfinancial firms rose from about 23% in 2013 to about 31% in 2022.

Why intangibles are "missing" from many balance sheets

  • Although intangibles are likely to yield future benefits, it is difficult to reliably measure those benefits.
  • Many U.S. balance sheets are "missing" valuable intangible assets.
  • Even though many intangible assets are not on the balance sheet, they have tremendous economic value.
  • This can explain part of the wide disparity between a company's market value and the book value of its stockholders' equity. The median market-to-book ratio for S&P 500 companies rose from roughly 2.2 in 2009 to a peak near 4.8 in 2021, falling to about 3.8 in 2022.

Cullowhee examples

The review above uses the lecture and textbook examples. Here are the same ideas with Cullowhee Cycle Works.

Cost flow and FIFO

Cullowhee had 12,000 packs available at a total cost of $4,965,000, and 1,000 packs remain. Under FIFO, the ending packs are the newest (Q4 at $440): ending inventory = $440,000 and COGS = 4,965,000 − 440,000 = $4,525,000.

Weighted-average cost

Average cost = 4,965,000 ÷ 12,000 = $413.75 per pack. Ending inventory = 1,000 × 413.75 = $413,750, and COGS = $4,551,250, between FIFO ($4,525,000) and LIFO ($4,585,000).

Capitalize or expense?

Assembly line ($ thousand): invoice 1,800 + freight 60 + installation 100 + test runs 40 = 2,000 capitalized. Worker training and the maintenance contract are expensed.

Straight-line depreciation

Assembly line: cost 2,000, salvage 100, life 10 years. Depreciation = (2,000 − 100) ÷ 10 = 190 a year. If the line runs for 3 months of FY2026, depreciation is 190 × 3/12 = 47.5.

Goodwill and acquired technology

Highlands Cell Packs ($ thousand): price 6,000 − (PP&E 1,700 + inventory 500 + technology 1,600) = goodwill 2,200. The technology has an 8-year life: 1,600 ÷ 8 = 200 a year, or 100 for the six months after July 1.
